articles.title: What Trump Has Built
articles.text:
Donald Trump struts onto the new White House helipad, an 80,000-sq.-ft. expanse of carved granite on the South Lawn. “Can you believe this?” he says, taking in the scene, the Washington Monument rising in the distance. The President lingers over the details of the project with obvious pleasure, pointing out the gray stone imported from Italy and describing how five separate sections were fitted together, with measurements he says are precise to an eighth of an inch.
Behind him rises a bigger renovation project: the new White House ballroom, its concrete skeleton consuming the former East Wing. Lawsuits have followed the endeavor, alleging that Trump demolished the historic structure and began building its replacement without congressional authorization or the required federal reviews. He kept building anyway. Trump points to the walls, calling them “nuclear concrete” (the sort, he says, used in nuclear facilities), and describes a military complex beneath the ballroom that will plunge six stories underground. There will be five separate floors, he says, with one side made entirely of glass, 6 or 8 in. thick. He holds his hands apart to demonstrate. “The steel goes up next week.” 
As we walk toward the Oval Office, Trump stops several times to inspect his handiwork. There are freshly painted doors, new gold doorknobs, the Rose Garden lawn ripped out and replaced with a Mar-a-Lago-style patio, where he now presides over dinners at what he calls the Rose Garden Club. “People say, why do you spend so much time on this?” he says. “But I find it relaxing.” Later, he returns to the subject again. “It’s what I do best,” he muses aloud. “I say, am I a better builder or a politician?”
One can understand Trump’s fixation on his construction projects. At one of the lowest points of his presidency, he is absorbed with the physical details of a world he can remake to his liking. There is something revealing in the contrast. Here, he can still point to a wall and say how thick it should be, decide where the grass ends and the stone begins, make demands and have them fulfilled. With his presidency seemingly spinning off course, Trump has busied himself with things he can control.
Outside these gates, events have become increasingly resistant to Trump’s will. The war in Iran, launched without congressional authorization and initially described by Trump as a four-to-six-week undertaking, is seven months old when we meet, with no end in sight. It has sent oil and gasoline prices soaring and convulsed the global economy. Inflationary pressures compounded by Trump’s tariffs have pushed the Federal Reserve—now led by his handpicked chairman—to raise interest rates over his objections, with another hike possible before year’s end. Mortgage rates have climbed to 7.5%, worsening an already punishing housing market.
The political coalition that returned Trump to power has frayed, with signs of discontent among independents, rural voters, and parts of the Latino electorate, even as his GOP base remains substantially loyal. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in September put his approval at 32%, the lowest of his political career; a recent Wall Street Journal survey recorded the lowest ratings of any President heading into midterm elections since 1990. Republican candidates have distanced themselves from his military actions and his deportation campaign. Voters have recoiled at his laissez-faire approach to the artificial intelligence industry and his accumulation of wealth while in office through crypto deals, thousands of disclosed stock trades, and an expanding empire of Trump-branded developments stretching from Saudi Arabia and Qatar to India and Vietnam.
Inside the Administration, senior advisers increasingly recognize that he has passed the apogee of his second-term power. Across the Republican Party, officials are preparing for the likelihood of losing the House—and perhaps the Senate—in the midterms. After two years spent almost entirely on offense, Trump may soon be forced onto defense. Democratic control of Congress would bring investigations and subpoenas, hearings, and potentially a third round of impeachment proceedings. Cabinet officials could be hauled before Congress. Trump describes the prospect in characteristic terms. “They’ll probably go after me,” he says, “and I’ll go after them.”
Yet with so much at stake—for the country and the world, for his party and his own power—Trump can seem curiously preoccupied. During a 75-minute Oval Office interview with TIME, he was discursive and grievance-fueled, veering from the crises of his presidency to resentments old and emerging. He said he regretted appointing Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, after they ruled against him on tariffs, mail ballots, and birthright citizenship. “I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.” On his expectation of fealty, he was unapologetic: “I do like loyalty, yeah.” Again and again, he returned to the condition of the White House itself, complaining that his predecessors had left the building in disrepair and deriding Barack Obama as someone who “doesn’t know if something’s dirty or clean.”
Trump dismissed widespread opposition to the rapid build-out of data centers, including among his own base, as a prescription for a poorer America. When pressed on the limits of his power, Trump left himself ample room: He would not rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms, nor promise to refrain from bringing wrecking balls to the Kennedy Center without congressional approval. “I’m not committing to anything,” he says. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”
In Trump’s telling, he is simply doing what has to be done, even when that means breaking foundational promises to his voters. He campaigned as a president of peace, but is now waging a war he says was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He points to Venezuela, where his removal of Nicolás Maduro and the elevation of Delcy Rodríguez have brought the country into Washington’s orbit, as proof that his projection of U.S. power can produce results. He touts most-favored-nation drug pricing and restricting institutional investors from buying single-family homes as measures that will lower costs for Americans. New GDP and inflation figures suggest the economy remains strong.
When asked why he remains consumed with construction projects so removed from the country’s concerns, Trump offers a rationale: “The White House is a very special symbol. It’s a symbol of America. It’s a symbol of our greatness.” He speaks of his building projects in the language of legacy—monuments meant to endure long after he is gone. But while Trump obsesses over stonework and fixtures, gold and glass, the more important parts of his legacy are being built too—in the decisions he makes from inside these walls, and the consequences unfolding far beyond them. 
In late April, the President summoned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a retinue of military and national security officials to the Oval Office. By Trump’s own timeline, the war with Iran was supposed to be over already, with a new regime in place and a nuclear program throttled. But the Islamic Republic had proved resilient and resourceful, choking off oil through the Strait of Hormuz and sending tremors through the global economy.
Now there was another problem. Trump had learned from a New York Times report that the U.S. military was running low on certain munitions after firing more than 1,200 Patriot missile interceptors. To replenish the losses, the Pentagon was drawing on assets stationed in Asia and Europe, potentially weakening American defenses in other theaters. “What the f-ck is this?” Trump said to Hegseth, according to two officials familiar with the exchange, handing him a printout of the story.
According to those officials, Hegseth borrowed one of Trump’s favorite terms of derision, telling the President it was “fake news.” The Secretary of Defense insisted that the reporters had taken the facts out of context and exaggerated them to make the Administration look bad. But the reporting emerged from an official DOD inspector general’s assessment. (A spokesperson for Hegseth denied the exchange.)
Trump’s frustration went beyond munition stores. The war was polling miserably. At the time, 13 U.S. service members had been killed and nearly 400 wounded. (Those numbers would increase to 19 killed and more than 800 wounded by the end of September.) Gasoline prices had risen more than 40% since the opening attacks on Feb. 28. The conflict had already cost more than $25 billion, and the consequences were beginning to bleed into the midterm campaign. The President found himself without an exit ramp. That dynamic appears to hold true: Instead of concluding the war, Trump tells TIME, he may ramp up the bombing after the midterms if they can’t reach a satisfactory deal. “Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world,” he says. “With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”
In recent months, Trump’s relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has grown more acrimonious, according to a senior Administration official. Netanyahu urged Trump toward war with Tehran but has since complicated Trump’s efforts to end it, including by striking Hezbollah targets in Lebanon after Trump told him not to, multiple U.S. officials tell TIME. Trump says he does not believe reports that Netanyahu was warned by Egypt and the UAE ahead of the Oct. 7 attacks, but stops short of endorsing him for re-election as Israelis prepare to vote in late October for the first time since the worst security failure in the country’s history. Asked whether he might work better with Netanyahu’s leading challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, Trump leaves the possibility open. “Well, I don’t know,” he says. “I don’t hear bad things about him.”
The decision to attack Iran was a hinge point in Trump’s second term. His first year back in power had unfolded as a frenetic exercise in presidential will, a barrage of executive actions and dismantled guardrails that had largely gone according to plan. Then his second year opened with the raid on Caracas and capture of Maduro, a daring operation that reinforced Trump’s conviction that audacity could succeed where caution had failed. The subsequent attack on Tehran would test the limits of that conviction—and reveal how quickly confidence born of success could lead to overreach.
A cascade of crises followed. Though Trump has dismissed the pain of rising gas prices, he concedes the war has depleted a subset of U.S. munitions. “Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms,” he says. Trump says he has struck deals with leading defense manufacturers, including Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, to replenish the arsenal and expand production. “They’re building four, five, six plants,” he says, citing Patriot and THAAD anti-ballistic-missile facilities. “They’re building tremendous amounts of capability.”
When asked what this will cost American taxpayers, Trump offers a curious metric: less, he says, than America makes in a single month from Venezuelan oil. Yet Americans have so far felt little benefit from that arrangement. Major U.S. oil companies have returned to Venezuela and begun extracting from the world’s largest proven crude reserves, but gas prices remain at record highs for September. Meanwhile, Trump’s tariff regime strained America’s global relationships and reverberated through the economy. 
Trump points to low unemployment, robust consumer spending, and a stock market at record highs as evidence that his economic program is working. By those measures, the economy has remained strong. But they coexist with a harsher reality: the cost of everyday life remains painfully high.
By summer, Trump was growing angrier with U.S. allies that had refused to come to America’s aid against Iran—from the European powers and South Korea to Canada. Trump has directed much of his ire over the issue at America’s neighbor to the north, according to a close aide. “He doesn’t like the fact that we essentially protect them because of their proximity to our military might, and doesn’t think they give us enough in return,” says a Trump senior adviser. On July 20, Trump invoked a 1930 statute to impose a 50% tariff on Canadian goods. The trade war with America’s second largest trading partner hit steel, aluminum, and lumber especially hard, disrupting supply chains and raising the cost of materials that went into everything from factories to new homes. 
Borrowing costs were becoming their own problem. For Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, preventing a sell-off in the bond market from becoming a broader crisis was an increasingly urgent task. By late September, only 25% of Americans believed Trump’s policies had improved the economy, according to a Wall Street Journal poll, while 60% said they had worsened it. Trump had returned to office promising cheaper energy, lower prices, and an economic boom. Instead, voters were finding the opposite. “It’s not lost on any of us,” a Trump adviser tells TIME. “When voters aren’t happy with the economy, they tend to vote against the party in charge.”
Since returning to office, Trump has marveled at AI’s capabilities. He is increasingly in thrall to the tech executives courting him. In December 2025, Elon Musk returned to the Oval Office for a clandestine meeting. Trump spent hours asking Grok, Musk’s AI chatbot, questions about his presidency and legacy, according to an official present. At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes against Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the U.S. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured Maduro. According to the official present, the chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall. After Trump ordered the mission to seize Maduro, the following month, celebrations broke out in the streets. Trump, according to officials, came away thinking Grok was ingenious.
Along with his fascination with the technology came two related concerns. One was economic: that enthusiasm for AI’s potential was propping up the stock market. The other was geopolitical, reinforced in conversations with industry titans such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: that China could gain a decisive advantage over the U.S. if it developed more powerful AI first. Trump was committed to giving American companies the freedom to build faster than their foreign competitors. That meant embracing the unprecedented infrastructure build-out required to support the industry’s computing needs. After watching a cable news segment about the backlash, Trump fired off a Truth Social post. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote Aug. 31. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” 
Days later, aides showed Trump surveys from his longtime pollster, Tony Fabrizio, showing pervasive anxiety about AI: fears of lost jobs, rising costs, and technology eventually escaping human control. Fellow Republicans facing voters in November were increasingly eager to put distance between themselves and the issue. Trump “really just didn’t seem to care,” one aide says. “He wants to do what he wants to do. He’s used to generating outrage and then watching everyone eventually crawl back to him. It’s hard to convince him to do anything at this point.”
Trump was unfazed by the burgeoning bipartisan calls for new AI regulations. “I don’t have to destroy the industry,” he says. “We’re making a lot of money with that industry. That industry is the Industrial Revolution, but bigger. It’s the internet, but much bigger.” The details don’t appear to concern him. When TIME asks about OpenAI agents’ meddling with federal government websites, Trump responds: “Who breached it? They’re not allowed to do that.”
Trump’s contribution to the debate about AI safeguards has been to announce the formation of an “AI Force,” which he now wants to rename the “SI Force”—part of his effort to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” Asked what the group will do, Trump responds: “It’s going to be super intelligent.” Pressed further, he explains that it will consist of industry leaders advising him on government policy. On Sept. 29, he met with AI leaders at the White House, where the President and top executives from six leading tech companies signed a “constitution” to police themselves—a covenant of self-regulation in lieu of government oversight. An Administration official present said they left with a “no surprises if something happens” understanding between the White House and the industry. 
It was an example of how Trump has surrounded himself with industry leaders, seeking their advice, favor, and political donations. A recent CNN poll found 75% of Americans viewed artificial intelligence with more fear and concern than excitement, with broad bipartisan support for greater federal oversight. But Trump waves away AI fears, placing them in a familiar catalogue of what he considers manufactured panics. “They said that our country was going to burn down because of global warming,” he says. “Then they changed the name to climate change because global warming turned out to be a hoax. Russia, Russia, Russia was a hoax.” Asked who, exactly, is perpetrating the supposed hoax of AI concern, Trump throws his hands in the air. “The whole country is based on fake stuff,” he says, “because these people have Trump derangement syndrome.”
Inside the Oval Office, Trump’s redesign is impossible to miss. There is gold everywhere, from the decorative plasterwork to the inscriptions on the ceiling and the gilded frames crowding the walls. The room is so dazzling you practically need sunglasses. Trumpian tchotchkes are scattered about: a FIFA “World Peace Prize” sits next to the Resolute Desk, where the President keeps a commendation given to his uncle during his years as an MIT professor. 
At times, Trump’s train of thought was difficult to keep up with, his conversation moving in streams and eddies before circling back to familiar obsessions. He recounted conversations that sometimes sounded improbable. At one point, Trump claimed the Secret Service had wanted to tear down the Oval Office and rebuild it, only for him to intervene. “I said, ‘My ass, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place.’”
Whatever happens in November, people close to Trump expect him to devote more of his remaining presidency to foreign affairs, as second-term Presidents often do, with particular attention to the western hemisphere, where ideologically sympathetic governments have given him opportunities to expand American influence. At home, they expect another emphasis altogether: Trump’s campaign against what he calls “lawfare” and his effort to reshape cultural institutions, including the nation’s museums, in his battle against what he calls “woke” ideology.
Looking ahead to the midterms, Trump dismisses unfavorable polls as fake and insists Republicans can prevail. “I think we’ll do OK if I campaign, and I intend to,” he says. So far, he has done little beyond a two-day midterm convention and a few fundraisers, but top advisers say the President is preparing a campaign sprint to help Republicans stave off disaster in the midterms: visiting 32 competitive districts in the next month, with the MAGA-style rallies that powered his political rise.
Inside the White House, advisers are already contemplating what a divided Washington would mean. “I think if the worst happens in the midterms, we’ll be forced to think more bipartisan,” one top official says. “I would hope that if we win, we can still do that, because for two years we’ve run a completely partisan play. When you’re looking back on your time, I don’t think that’s what you should be proud of, even if it was successful.”
Trump’s political operation boasts a $400 million war chest, but he has only recently begun opening his checkbook. Aides say he has been reluctant to spend because he wants to preserve cash for future elections as a means of keeping his grip on his party. “He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now,” a Trump aide told TIME this fall. “He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities.”
Aides are bracing for turnover after the midterms as Trump sheds officials who have frustrated him. A source close to the President says he has openly mused about firing the FBI Director Kash Patel and has expressed frustration with Hegseth. Trump says he intends to protect those who remain. When TIME asks whether he plans to issue pre-emptive pardons to aides and associates before Democrats—or a future Administration—can pursue them, he suggests he will, offering a familiar justification: “Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody.”
As the conversation moves between war and peace, his own grip on power, and the possibility of impeachment, Trump keeps returning to the trappings of the office. He asks Natalie Harp, his ever present aide, to bring in photographs of earlier White House construction projects, including renovations from the 1930s and the Truman-era reconstruction. He studies the pictures as evidence for his case, lamenting the judges and injunctions now complicating his own efforts. Holding up a photograph of work being performed on the State Dining Room in 1950, Trump complains about a judge he says accused him of destroying the White House. “It’s the sh-t I have to go through,” he says. 
Toward the end of our interview, I ask what he will miss most when his presidency is over. This time there is no digression, no grievance, no story. Trump does not need a moment to think: “This beautiful room.” 
—With reporting by Leslie Dickstein, Simmone Shah, and Olivia B. Waxman

articles.title: 8 lần Bamboo Airways thay chủ tịch trong hơn 4 năm
articles.text:
8 lần Bamboo Airways thay chủ tịch trong hơn 4 năm
(Dân trí) - Ông Lê Thái Sâm vừa trở lại làm Chủ tịch Bamboo Airways. Đây đã là lần thứ 8 hãng thay đổi nhân sự ở vị trí này kể từ đầu năm 2022.
Công ty cổ phần Hàng không Tre Việt (Bamboo Airways) mới đây cập nhật nội dung đăng ký doanh nghiệp, trong đó đáng chú ý là ông Lê Thái Sâm trở lại giữ chức Chủ tịch HĐQT, đồng thời là người đại diện theo pháp luật của hãng.
Ông Sâm trở lại vị trí cao nhất HĐQT Bamboo Airways sau hơn 10 tháng rời ghế. Tháng 11/2025, ông Bùi Quang Dũng được bầu làm Chủ tịch nhiệm kỳ 2023-2028 thay ông Sâm.
Sự trở lại lần này tiếp tục nối dài chuỗi biến động nhân sự cấp cao tại hãng hàng không. Kể từ khi ông Đặng Tất Thắng tiếp quản ghế Chủ tịch vào cuối tháng 3/2022, Bamboo Airways đã 8 lần thay đổi nhân sự giữ chức Chủ tịch HĐQT.
Chuỗi thay đổi bắt đầu từ cuối tháng 3/2022, sau khi ông Trịnh Văn Quyết rời vị trí Chủ tịch Bamboo Airways. Ông Đặng Tất Thắng sau đó đảm nhiệm ghế Chủ tịch HĐQT, đồng thời giữ chức Tổng giám đốc hãng.
Nhiệm kỳ của ông Thắng chỉ kéo dài khoảng 4 tháng. Cuối tháng 7/2022, ông xin từ nhiệm vì lý do cá nhân. Đến tháng 8 cùng năm, HĐQT Bamboo Airways bầu ông Nguyễn Ngọc Trọng giữ chức Chủ tịch. Ông Trọng là một trong những lãnh đạo gắn bó với hãng từ những ngày đầu thành lập, từng giữ vị trí Phó tổng giám đốc Vietnam Airlines trước khi gia nhập Bamboo Airways.
Ông Trọng giữ vị trí này khoảng 10 tháng. Đến tháng 6/2023, Bamboo Airways bước vào một đợt thay đổi lớn về bộ máy quản trị khi các thành viên HĐQT nhiệm kỳ cũ xin từ nhiệm. Tại ĐHĐCĐ thường niên ngày 21/6, ông Oshima Hideki - cựu lãnh đạo Japan Airlines - được bầu làm Chủ tịch HĐQT Bamboo Airways.
Tuy nhiên, ông Oshima chỉ ngồi ghế Chủ tịch trong thời gian rất ngắn. Ngày 11/7/2023, HĐQT Bamboo Airways chấp thuận đơn từ nhiệm chức vụ của ông cùng ba thành viên HĐQT khác. Ông Lê Thái Sâm được bầu làm Chủ tịch HĐQT, còn ông Oshima chuyển sang giữ chức Phó chủ tịch thường trực.
Đây cũng là giai đoạn cơ cấu cổ đông và bộ máy lãnh đạo Bamboo Airways có nhiều thay đổi. Tại thời điểm đó, ông Sâm được giới thiệu là sở hữu lượng cổ phần tương đương hơn 50% vốn điều lệ của hãng, khi tính cả số cổ phần nhận chuyển nhượng từ FLC và từ phương án hoán đổi nợ. Trước đó, tính đến ngày 10/4/2023, tổng số tiền Bamboo Airways vay của ông, gồm cả gốc và lãi, là hơn 7.727 tỷ đồng.
Đến tháng 2/2024, Bamboo Airways tiếp tục thay chủ tịch. HĐQT hãng bầu ông Phan Đình Tuệ giữ vị trí này nhiệm kỳ 2023-2028, còn ông Sâm chuyển sang làm Phó chủ tịch thường trực. Ông Tuệ từng giữ chức Phó tổng giám đốc Sacombank trước khi tham gia HĐQT Bamboo Airways vào năm 2023.
So với một số người tiền nhiệm, ông Tuệ có thời gian tại vị dài hơn, kéo dài đến giữa năm 2025. Tháng 6/2025, ông gửi đơn xin từ nhiệm.
Sau khi ông Tuệ rời vị trí, ông Phạm Ngọc Vịnh được bầu làm Chủ tịch Bamboo Airways vào tháng 7/2025. Tuy nhiên, nhiệm kỳ này cũng chỉ kéo dài hơn một tháng. Ngày 13/8, Bamboo Airways thông báo ông Vịnh từ nhiệm vì lý do cá nhân. Cùng ngày, HĐQT bầu ông Lê Thái Sâm trở lại làm Chủ tịch; ông Trương Phương Thành thay ông Lương Hoài Nam giữ chức Tổng giám đốc.
Đến tháng 11/2025, chiếc ghế Chủ tịch một lần nữa đổi chủ. Ông Bùi Quang Dũng, lãnh đạo Tập đoàn FLC, được bầu làm Chủ tịch Bamboo Airways thay ông Sâm. Ông Sâm khi đó vẫn tiếp tục là thành viên HĐQT.
Và sau hơn 10 tháng, đến ngày 30/9 năm nay, ông Sâm lại trở lại vị trí Chủ tịch.
Như vậy, trong hơn 4 năm kể từ khi ông Trịnh Văn Quyết rời ghế, vị trí Chủ tịch Bamboo Airways lần lượt trải qua các ông: Đặng Tất Thắng, Nguyễn Ngọc Trọng, Oshima Hideki, Lê Thái Sâm, Phan Đình Tuệ, Phạm Ngọc Vịnh, Lê Thái Sâm, Bùi Quang Dũng; và mới nhất là ông Lê Thái Sâm.

articles.title: The President and the Press
articles.text:
Berating reporters, revoking credentials, suing news organizations—hardly a week goes by without Donald Trump’s attacking the press. An experienced commander of headlines and inveterate consumer of media, he cajoles journalists one day and harangues them the next. But the man who preceded Trump as the President to appear most often on the cover of TIME reigned supreme in media manipulation too. Well before Trump railed against fake news, Richard Nixon waged a sustained campaign to intimidate and punish those who covered him.
The relationship between Presidents and the press is inherently adversarial. Since the emergence of a modern mass media and a professional White House press corps in the early 20th century, Presidents have sought to use journalists to disseminate their ideas, goals, and achievements—and have treated coverage that deviates from their spin as misleading, hostile, or malicious. Reporters, on the other hand, while recognizing their duty to relay what the President says and does, believe that they can offer a fuller, more accurate account of events than the White House does—by adding context, checking facts, and airing dissenting views. In that difference of perspective lies a recipe for conflict.
Every President has warred with journalists. Theodore Roosevelt sued Joseph Pulitzer’s New York World for alleging corruption in the purchase of the Panama Canal. (He lost.) Franklin Roosevelt instructed an impertinent correspondent to don a dunce cap and stand in the corner. Dwight Eisenhower baldly lied to the press after the Soviet Union shot down an American spy plane. Barack Obama tried to exclude Fox News from an interview with the other TV networks and used the Espionage Act to pursue leakers. The list goes on.
But, at least until Trump, no other President had a more contentious relationship with the media than Nixon. By the time he took office in 1969, the White House–press relationship had grown sharply combative, thanks to the Vietnam War, Lyndon Johnson’s “credibility gap,” and the cultural upheavals and suspicion of authority that marked the 1960s. Journalists took it for granted that Nixon, with his long history of resenting the press, had nefarious designs on neutering the Fourth Estate. The venerated CBS anchorman Walter Cronkite labeled Nixon’s antipress campaign “a grand conspiracy.” Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee charged that “the First Amendment is in greater danger than any time I’ve seen it.” A National Press Club report found Nixon guilty of “an unprecedented, government-wide effort to control, restrict and conceal information” and “discredit the press.” And all of this happened before impeachment proceedings even began.
The relationship was not exclusively hostile. As with all administrations, there were ups and downs. At times, even as they distrusted him personally, reporters showered Nixon with admiring coverage, such as during the summer of 1972 when détente was easing tensions with the Soviet Union and after Nixon made his breakthrough trip to communist China. That summer, according to press critic Ben Bagdikian’s count, of more than 2,200 Washington correspondents, only about a dozen pursued the emerging Watergate story. Nixon coasted to re-election.
Yet these bouts of positive coverage did little to appease Nixon, whose antipress campaign continued unabated. Some of the President’s men later owned up to zealotry. “We used to watch the news broadcasts and go up the walls at what we thought was unfair coverage of Nixon,” recalled Chuck Colson, who in the fall of 1972 bullied CBS executives into shortening the second part of a Watergate exposé. Speechwriter Ray Price said flatly, “We did often lie, mislead, deceive, try to use [the press], and to con them.” William Safire, another speechwriter, recalled Nixon insisting that “the press is the enemy ... to be hated and beaten”—an attitude Safire called “neither justifiable nor defensible” and yet deeply held.
The particular skirmishes in Nixon’s war on journalists would fill not only a ledger but a shelf of books. (In writing my own book about Nixon, I consumed at least a dozen books on the subject, with titles like The Chilling Effect in TV News: Intimidation by the Nixon White House and The Engineering of Restraint: The Nixon Administration and the Press.) Some of the Administration’s offenses appear in retrospect fairly routine or mild, like the maddening evasiveness of press secretary Ron Ziegler, or even Vice President Spiro Agnew’s baroque diatribes in which he lashed out at the power of the TV networks and major newspapers. But others were genuinely disturbing assaults on the independence of the press corps, waged by a man loath to acknowledge any constraints on his power.
One of the earliest of these was Nixon’s plan, hatched with National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger, to stop leaks by wiretapping the homes and phones of journalists who reported critically on the Administration’s actions, starting with the 1969 bombing of North Vietnamese sanctuaries in Cambodia, which the White House had hoped to keep secret. At the Georgetown home of syndicated columnist Joseph Kraft, another targeted newsman, White House hireling John J. Ragan, wearing a repairman’s uniform, climbed up a nearby telephone pole to install a battery-operated transmitter that would convey every conversation on the Kraft family phone to a tape recorder in the trunk of a car parked close by. The wiretaps on Kraft and other reporters, installed without any warrant, wouldn’t be exposed until just before the 1973 Watergate hearings, but they were later found to be unconstitutional infringements on the journalists’ rights.
The wiretapping scheme grew out of Nixon and Kissinger’s mania for clamping down on leaks that might damage the Administration’s standing. That mania resurfaced in 1971, after the New York Times published the Pentagon Papers, a Defense Department study of American involvement in the Vietnam War. Told by Kissinger that he would be seen as a “weakling” if he didn’t respond, the President had his Attorney General sue the Times to force it to stop publishing the classified documents. No previous Administration had ever tried to impose “prior restraint”—government censorship prohibiting the publication of material before it appears. Eventually, in a landmark First Amendment case, the Supreme Court rejected Nixon’s claim that national security justified the suppression of the information. But the Pentagon Papers leak had other consequences too: it spurred the White House to create the so-called Plumbers unit—plumbers, after all, fix leaks—that would soon engage in a battery of illegal activities, including the break-ins at the Democratic headquarters at the Watergate complex in 1972.
Nixon also used the power of the Executive Branch to punish news outlets he considered unfriendly. The Washington Post Co. at the time owned two Florida television stations, WJXT in Jacksonville and WPLG in Miami, whose licenses were regulated by the Federal Communications Commission. Furious that the Post was digging into Watergate, Nixon fumed to his aides H.R. Haldeman and John Dean in September 1972, “The Post is going to have damnable, damnable problems out of this one. They have a television station ... and they’re going to have to get it renewed ... the game has to be played awfully rough.” Soon thereafter, allies of Nixon challenged the Post’s ownership of those licenses—challenges that failed but that hurt the company’s stock price and cost it huge legal fees.
Individuals, too, faced retribution. White House correspondent Martin Schram of Newsday, who had reported on Nixon’s dubious financial entanglements with his shady friend Bebe Rebozo, was excluded from the President’s historic 1972 China trip. CBS News’ Daniel Schorr endured an FBI investigation after a negative piece about Nixon’s pledge to help Catholic parochial schools. Nixon often told aides to have the IRS audit his journalistic detractors; some of these enemies were audited, although direct links to the President’s instructions were hard to prove. Nixon and his confidants also discussed taking revenge on syndicated journalist Jack Anderson, a regular thorn in the Administration’s side. G. Gordon Liddy, the resident wild man of Nixon’s re-election team, at one point plotted in all seriousness to have the columnist assassinated, even enlisting a CIA poison expert to help with the planning. Saner heads quashed the plan.
Nixon’s war on the media ultimately failed. The courts rebuffed his attempt to censor the Pentagon Papers. Congress exposed many of his illegal and covert operations. Watergate showed the value of investigative journalism in holding a lawless President accountable. But Watergate also heightened journalists’ propensity to distrust power and embrace a confrontational posture, sometimes manifested in productive reporting but as often evident in a reflexively snide, captious tone. Presidents, meanwhile, if not matching Nixon in their sheer hostility toward the media, followed him in viewing reporters as adversaries to be monitored, punished, and discredited. In that sense, Donald Trump simply inherited a playbook bequeathed by Nixon.

articles.title: Doanh nghiệp tự quyết giá xăng dầu, có lo ‘loạn giá’?
articles.text:
Theo dự thảo nghị định kinh doanh xăng dầu đang được Bộ Công thương hoàn thiện, dự kiến trình Chính phủ trong tuần tới, doanh nghiệp được tự quyết giá xăng dầu.
Theo đó, giá xăng dầu bán lẻ công bố sẽ áp dụng theo công thức của cơ quan quản lý nhà nước: giá bán = giá mua + chi phí tạo nguồn + chi phí kinh doanh định mức + lợi nhuận + thuế. Trong đó, giá mua và chi phí tạo nguồn do thương nhân tự xác định theo thực tế kinh doanh.
Tuy nhiên, xung quanh đề xuất trên vẫn còn nhiều ý kiến băn khoăn nguy cơ xảy ra tình trạng "loạn giá" trên thị trường?
Trả về đúng cơ chế thị trường, người tiêu dùng hưởng lợi
Chia sẻ với Thanh Niên, ông Trịnh Quanh Khanh, Phó chủ tịch thường trực kiêm Tổng thư ký Hiệp hội Xăng dầu Việt Nam, nhận định việc giao quyền tự quyết giá thực chất là trả xăng dầu về đúng nguyên lý vận hành của thị trường. Khi đó, thị trường sẽ chấp nhận hiện tượng "giá mấp mô", tức là các doanh nghiệp khác nhau có thể công bố mức giá bán lẻ chênh lệch nhau.
"Người tiêu dùng hoàn toàn có quyền lựa chọn. Cùng một địa bàn, cây xăng này bán 10 đồng, cây xăng kia bán 10,2 đồng thì người dân sẽ tự quyết định mua ở đâu. Giá bán lẻ lúc này không chỉ phản ánh giá vốn mà còn phụ thuộc vào uy tín thương hiệu, chất lượng dịch vụ, thái độ phục vụ và việc niêm yết bán đúng, bán đủ", ông Khanh phân tích.
Ngoài ra, ông Khanh lưu ý giá xăng dầu trong nước vẫn chịu sự chi phối từ tín hiệu giá thế giới, vận hành theo công thức tính giá chung và Nhà nước vẫn nắm công cụ quản lý thông qua việc kiểm tra, giám sát giá xăng dầu doanh nghiệp tự công bố hay các kịch bản bình ổn. Do đó, thị trường không thể biến tướng thành bức tranh tự do nâng giá vô căn cứ.
Đồng quan điểm, ông Nguyễn Văn Đức, Phó giám đốc Công ty CP xăng dầu dầu khí Thái Nguyên, cho rằng việc doanh nghiệp tự quyết giá sẽ tạo ra môi trường cạnh tranh lành mạnh. Bản chất cạnh tranh là doanh nghiệp nào tối ưu được chi phí vận hành, bộ máy gọn nhẹ thì sẽ đưa ra mức giá tốt hơn.
"Sẽ không có chuyện hai cây xăng gần nhau mà bán chênh lệch giá quá lớn vì không ai mua ở nơi giá cao.
Giảm trung gian tạo dư địa hạ giá xăng dầu
Theo ông Trần Hữu Linh, Cục trưởng Cục Quản lý và Phát triển thị trường trong nước, khoảng 10 - 15 năm qua, hệ thống phân phối xăng dầu có quá nhiều tầng nấc. Mỗi khâu trung gian lại phát sinh thêm chi phí, vận hành kém hiệu quả.
Trong dự thảo mới, hệ thống kinh doanh xăng dầu được tổ chức lại theo hướng chỉ còn 2 loại hình thương nhân chính là thương nhân đầu mối và thương nhân phân phối.
Tại hội nghị góp ý dự thảo nghị định do Bộ Công thương tổ chức ngày 30.9, các chuyên gia, đại diện các doanh nghiệp cho rằng, cùng với cơ chế doanh nghiệp được tự quyết giá bán, khi thu gọn bộ máy phân phối, cắt giảm các tầng nấc trung gian, mua bán lòng vòng giúp loại bỏ nhiều khoản chi phí không cần thiết sẽ tạo dư địa giảm giá bán lẻ xăng dầu.
Ông Trần Hữu Linh khẳng định dự thảo nghị định lần này hướng đến 3 mục tiêu cốt lõi. Thị trường xăng dầu được tái cấu trúc để tinh gọn hệ thống cung ứng, giảm các tầng nấc trung gian, giảm chi phí và thủ tục hành chính nhưng vẫn bảo đảm nguồn cung ổn định và hiệu quả.
Nhà nước trao quyền định giá cho thị trường và doanh nghiệp. Nhà nước xây dựng công thức, quy định những yếu tố chi phí thuộc phạm vi quản lý và thực hiện hậu kiểm; doanh nghiệp chủ động quyết định giá bán theo cơ chế thị trường.
Chuyển đổi số triệt để trong quản trị xăng dầu, kết nối dữ liệu về nhập, xuất, tồn, hóa đơn và lưu thông trên thị trường để nâng cao tính minh bạch và khả năng quản lý theo thời gian thực.
"Khi nghị định mới có hiệu lực, dữ liệu về nhập, xuất, tồn, lưu thông trên thị trường và hóa đơn sẽ từng bước được kết nối trực tuyến với hệ thống quản lý.
Bộ Công thương đang xây dựng ứng dụng để người tiêu dùng có thể biết thông tin về các cửa hàng, vị trí, chủng loại, giá xăng dầu và các dịch vụ đi kèm để người tiêu dùng thuận tiện lựa chọn", ông Linh thông tin.

articles.title: Read TIME’s ‘What Trump Has Built’ Interview Transcript
articles.text:
President Donald Trump sat down for an interview with TIME at the White House on Sept. 28.
Over the course of the interview, Trump discussed a wide range of issues, including the war with Iran, the artificial intelligence boom, the Federal Reserve, the Supreme Court, and his outlook for the midterms.
Below is a lightly edited transcript of the interview conducted by TIME Senior Political Correspondent Eric Cortellessa and Editor-in-Chief Sam Jacobs. Click here to read our fact check.
Read TIME's interview with President Donald Trump and the fact-check of that conversation.
TIME: I'm curious about your dinner last night with Dario.
Trump: Oh.
Yes, exactly. Do you still disagree with his views on what he calls AI safety?
I spoke to him about his views, and they're much different, I think, than what is portrayed in the media. First of all, I liked him and his wife a lot. They had dinner, and we were going to meet at 7:00. But I was at the big Presidents Cup. I was the chairman of it in Chicago at Marion, which is great. Actually, that was yeah, Medinah, at Medinah, last year, Marion, this time of year, it was really great, and so I called, I said, "Could we make it a little bit later?" He actually saw the helicopter land, so we made it a little bit later. We got in at about 10. We stayed for more than two hours, talked about a lot of things. Very smart guy. Maybe different than I thought, a little bit. Really a little bit different. But no, he understands.
Look, I say, if you're going to seek regulation, they can put you out of business. Now you do have to be responsible for yourself, and there aren't a lot of people that understand what's going on. This is a new one that is much different than people have ever seen before. But my attitude is, we're winning against the world by a lot, and I want to keep winning. There are those that say it's bigger than the industrial revolution, and you would think not. But actually, if you look at the numbers—you ever see these numbers? They're like, they're like straight up in the air. And from our standpoint, we have trillions of dollars being invested in our country because it's probably the biggest business there is. We're the most advanced, we have the, we have the smartest people. And tomorrow I have a big meeting. We have everybody. All the—Dario's coming back.
I'm curious what exactly is going on with all these meetings with these AI leaders.
Well, look, you know, this isn't like I'm building a building, which I can do out of my back pocket. It's easier to do that for me, and it's what I've been doing. This is a whole new world, probably mostly good, but some bad too. And it's a very powerful world. It's a very—potentially really could be good for medical. I mean, some of the things they're coming up with now that they never even thought about. But with good comes bad, and we want them, we want all of them to behave for themselves. Tomorrow's meeting. What time is that meeting tomorrow? Two?
Natalie Harp: Noon, in the East Room.
Trump: So we have everybody. Give me a list of the people at the meeting.
Can I ask, Mr. President?
We had a good evening the other night, three nights ago, or two nights ago.
Given the news this week, I have to ask: Why should Americans believe that you respect the free press when you're restricting access of some of our colleagues to the White House?
No, but say it a little louder.
Why should Americans believe that you respect the free press when you're restricting access to the White House to some of our colleagues?
Because I do respect the free press, but I don't respect fake news. I'll give you an example. CNN and MSDNC, which is MS Now—they changed the name because it does so poorly. But I won the election. I won it handily by massive numbers. I won the popular vote. I won all seven swing states. They said if you won three swing states, I won all seven. I won the counties. It's very important, 86% popular vote. Everything, and very conclusively, I haven't had a good story on CNN for years. They're incapable of being—they're fake news. Same thing on MS NOW.
If I do the finest thing, if I found the cure to cancer, they would say, "Why didn't he move quicker?" They are just horrible people, and they're so bad. So I believe in a free press. I believe in an honest press, but I don't believe in fake news. And I know it's fake because I know the thing—I don't mind, you know, if I do something wrong, I don't mind having a bad story. He's written a couple of times about something. I said, well listen, he’s not wrong. But with the press, if somebody's going to call me, if every single story is—look, I've done a lot of good stuff. I'm in the Oval Office. I mean, the public is very smart. If I wasn't doing a good job, I wouldn't have won that election by a lot.
Are you going to ignore the courts when they say this this denial is—
Well, the court actually said that, if you look at the judge's decision, he's been a very anti-Trump judge, which is very interesting. But if you look at his decision, he really said process. He talked about—come back to us with process.
He's a Trump-appointed judge. He was appointed by you.
Yeah, he was. He was. It's one of those things.
You don't think you're ignoring what he ordered you to do? You don't think you're ignoring his order?
No, I'm not. I'm not ignoring his order. I'm just saying that when I don't have to go out of my way, these people write only bad stories. When they say orders, what order? I'm not even aware.
Steven Cheung: The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that's different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.
Trump: He actually said to the premises of the White House?
Can I just ask, why now? You've had this contentious relationship with the media for a while. What was the impetus to doing this at this moment in time?
Well, it's just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I've got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it's not only CNN, and it's not only MSDNC. It's a lot of other people.
Let's talk a little bit about the war in Iran.
Just to finish.
Yeah, absolutely.
Because I don't think anybody should be forced to bear fake news, constantly bad stories, because I've done great things. I mean, I've done Venezuela. I've done—I can name, I can name 100 great things I've done. I never get good press. I never get fair press. Doesn’t have to be good. All it has to be is fair. So at a certain point, you say, "What's the purpose of like this crazy Kaitlan Collins?" She's a very average person. She's the most unhappy young person I've ever seen. If I did something spectacular by any standard, and they would write about it, they will only write badly. Sometimes I'm amazed at how they can—you know, yesterday I got tremendous applause from massive crowds that came to Duncan. And I said to the people, "Don't feel bad tomorrow when you read that I got booed out of the place." I didn't get booed out of the place.
I went to Tennessee. The crowd went wild. I went to, yesterday, to Chicago. Got the big golf tent. President’s coming. The crowd went absolutely wild. And I said—I didn’t want to make a big deal out of it but I just said a few words before the guy started playing. They asked me to make a speech. I said, "I'm not going to make a speech. I want to play golf." But I said to him—I mean, they had to stop the crowd from—they were going crazy, 100%. There was no negative number. Did anybody write anything negative about it? Check it out.
Isn't it a founding principle of the country that the press is supposed to hold government and those in power accountable? Do you believe in that?
It is, but they got to treat you fairly. You know, when they write stories that are knowingly false, and everyone knows NBC's, NBC's bad too, but CNN is terrible. MS Now changed their name because they have no friends.
Well, let's shift to Iran because a lot's going on over there. You initially said that the war would take about six to eight weeks. We're now entering the seventh month. Can you just explain, like, why is it taking so long?
Only because I wanted to go further. I took them out. I could have stopped then, but I wanted to go further. I didn't want them—because I met my timeline. If you look at what I did when we bombed the sites with a b2 bomber. Like we bombed those sites, and I call it nuclear dust—was under 1000s of tons of rubble. I could have stopped there, and I felt it was just inappropriate because—and they were itching to go on with their lives, if not there, someplace else. And so I went further. They're doing very poorly. Their economy is gone. Their inflation is at 300% or something like that. Their navy is gone. Their air force is gone. Everything's gone, and they want to make a deal, but I want to make the real deal. But when I said I was going to be there for a short period of time, I was, and then I decided I wanted to go further than that because I didn't want to have them come back in some different form.
Do you think the American people misunderstood that? I feel like most people heard you say four to six weeks.
No, I think the press fed it to them, so that—look, we were in Vietnam for 21, 20, years. We were in Afghanistan for many years. We were in Korea for many. We're everywhere for many years. I'm in there now for six months, and I've destroyed their nuclear capability. I've destroyed their navy, 159 ships are at the bottom of the sea. I've destroyed their air force. All their planes are gone. I've destroyed their radar. That's why you know we have, we had more ships come through last night. We had more barrels of oil come through last night than at any time in the history of the Strait. Last night we set a record.
Well, on that note, were you aware in February that they would likely—they being Tehran—were likely to retaliate by closing the Strait of Hormuz?
There was always a threat they had, and it worked for a little while. But we basically closed it on them. You know, they said we're going to close. I said, "Well, you close it, you're going to have big trouble." We took it over. You have to see the coastline. Everything is obliterated. They don't have radar. They don't have any anti-aircraft capability. Nothing. I have The New York Times saying how well they're doing, and it's so crazy. Their whole military is gone. Their radar is gone. Their leaders are gone. You know, we went through two levels of leaders, and The New York Times keeps writing about how well they're doing. They have no money. They have no value of money. They have nothing going, and just fake news, fake news, and maybe they’ll be next.
Last week, you said you might annihilate Iran. That was the word you used.
Yeah, I would do that. It's possible.
You've made versions of that threat before. You've also called yourself the president of peace.
Yeah.
How can the president of peace be calling for the annihilation of an entire people?
Because by annihilating Iran, we've created peace in the world. With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace.
Are you talking specifically about the government, the Islamic Republic regime? What about the innocent people?
They killed 75,000 people in the last number of months. Protesters, innocent [unintelligible], a lot of very good people. They killed 70, anywhere from 72 to 75,000. We all documented. They went on Brett Baier the other day and they lied about it. They said 3,000. Brett Bair said, “You got to be kidding, me!” No, they killed 75,000 people. It's unbelievable. It's a bloodbath. So we'll see. And the reason people don't rise up, because they're afraid of being killed. You know, they go out in the street and they end up killing 1,000 people, 2,000, sometimes less. They use snipers to go right through their head, and when—remember the women went, they had 500,000 women, and then they started getting hit by snipers right in the middle of their head? The women looked and they saw that, then they saw another one, and they ran like hell.
Do you regret not going into Iran or doing some sort of operation last January when there were these protests in the street and you said help is on the way?
No, I think we've done an incredible job with that. Now, so in Vietnam, when those massive numbers of people…in Afghanistan, likewise, went on forever. I fought two wars, and one person is too many. But I fought two wars that we lost 18 people. One was Venezuela, and the Venezuela one is incredible.
We're going to come to that.
We're selling millions of barrels of oil—that's ours—and it's been amazing. But we fought that war, it was less than one day. It was over. We're doing very well in Iran too. But it's a much bigger area, much bigger country, much further away. And—but the result is going to be the same. They want to make a deal. As soon as I make a deal, oil prices will drop to what they were. You know, when I was—you've heard me say this—When I was part of the going in, I was in Iowa, helping them campaign a little bit for the thing that we have coming up. And in Iowa, I mean, it was—oil was $1.90. I mean, it was like almost nothing. We broke the $2 barriers. One station was $1.85. One was $1.95. One was $1.99, and it was coming down all over the country. Now California is a little bit fictitious because in California they judge every time you lower the oil, they judge that. But I had no other way down there. And then I said to my people, including him, I said, "I hate to do this, you guys, but we have to take the nuclear weapon away from you."
Well, last on this question, over the weekend you rejected a ceasefire proposal from the Iranians. Can you just tell us why you did that?
Because things that I wouldn't have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.
Can you give us an example?
I mean, it was—they made an offer to open up the Strait. You know, you saw some aspects of it, not all. But it's just, it's just, it's not good enough. Nearly.
Are you going to ramp up bombing after the midterms? There's been reports of that.
Possible.
Are you considering that?
I can't tell you that because look, you know, you're asking, where are you going to bomb?
But it's in consideration?
We have a lot of weapons. You know, we've been stocking up for the last six months. Biden gave away massive amounts of munitions to Ukraine. Much more so than what we spent, and—but we're in great shape. And we're in great shape, but we're also now stocking up big and making—and we're keeping it. So if not him, then who?
I believe it was the worst speech. In fact, I put out a statement after I heard him, remember, saying that Gavin Newsom has just given up the presidency today. I believe it was the worst interview I've ever seen a professional politician—
Can we also ask about the building that you're doing? You showed us the helipad, the new ballroom, which you say is ahead of schedule. We can see it being constructed.
Everything I do is ahead of schedule.
Can you explain to people who say that these building projects don't have a connection to Americans who are struggling to pay bills? Why is this important for the American people?
So the White House is a very special symbol. It's a symbol of America. It's a symbol of our greatness. It's, I think, maybe the most important symbol that we have. The White House was a dump. The moldings were falling off the outside of the building. It hadn't been painted in…it was just a disgraceful dump. The doors were falling off. The locks were broken. And I said, I got to fix it. And I do that better than anybody else. Maybe I do it better than anything I do, and it's easy for me. It's actually relaxing. You know, for a lot of people, it drives them crazy.
For me, it’s relaxing. You see…And then the generals came. They said, Sir, they have new helicopters. I didn't buy them. Stupid Joe Biden, but they're very big and very powerful. They ripped the shit out of the grass, and I said—and they didn't know what to do, so they're going to use the old helicopters just for this one stop because they land on the grass. And I said, “Did you ever hear of building a helipad?” And everybody said, “Oh, what a wonderful idea. I never thought of that.” I said, "Why don't you design a helipad that's appropriate for these large helicopters?" And I built it. You see how I built it ahead of schedule.
You know how much money I spent on it? Zero. I got it from the company that built the helicopters, Lockheed, to build a helipad—close to $10 million—because they sold those helicopters and they didn't say you can't fly on grass. So I said to them, “Fellas, do you mind paying for it?” So I got it built for—I built it, but I built it with their money. The ballroom had $400 million in it. I had a judge who was a lunatic, and he said that I used the money in order to avoid getting a permit. I didn't. I don't own it. I'll be in it for just a relatively short period of time. Other guys will be in it for four years, seven years, eight years.
You take great pride—
And I had a judge that actually accused me of giving $400 million to go with that loan because I wanted to avoid permits. It's the craziest thing.
Are you willing to demolish the Kennedy Center?
It's in terrible shape. I'd be willing to save it, but it's in terrible, terrible shape. Only I can save it, and I'll tell you the biggest problem with the Kennedy Center. I can build it, but it will lose like many of those places. If you look at Carnegie Hall, New York, and all these places, the artsy places, they lose tens of millions of dollars. The Kennedy Center, long before I got there, was losing hundreds of millions of dollars. Do you know that? And if I'm going to go out and put up the money myself or raise that kind of money, I think the Trump Administration should be recognized. It's not just a building. I have $258 million. That's money to build. I got that, I got that from Congress. But the problem isn't that. The problem—and I'll make it nice. The problem isn't that.
The problem is that once it's built, as all houses of the art are doing, they lose—if you look at Carnegie Hall, if you look at some of the places like that, their numbers, they all lose a lot of money. The Kennedy Center was losing over the years hundreds of millions of dollars. Now I'm in a unique position. I'm a really good builder. I can fix it. I can fix it. And I'm also real rich where I can—and I have influence where I can put up money and I can also raise money. But we're talking about $60 to $125 million a year.
So, would you commit to not bringing in wrecking balls to Washington to demolish the Kennedy Center without the consent of Congress?
I'm not committing to anything. We're going to see how it plays out in court. But if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I'm going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people so they can see free—do you know the orchestra at the Kennedy Center? Do you know how much it costs for it? $22 million a year, that I've been paying. $22 million. It's a lot of money, and I said, if I'm going to do this, then I think the Trump Administration should be recognized.
And the judge is a Trump hater, radical left Trump hater. His wife uses a different name. Said. "No, you can't do that. Well, why would I want to stick with something that's going to lose hundreds of millions of dollars, and I'm not even recognized? It's not me; it's the administration. So I have people. He works hard on it. I have people that work hard on that because it's a financial loser. Always will be. Always has been. When I took it over, it was in extremely bad shape physically. The steel was rusted and rotted. The place was a dirty—like the White House. I fixed the White House, you know.
So, I get $550,000 a year as president. For the first term, I gave it. And I contributed to the White House renovation. I've done a great job. You would have come here a year ago, you would have seen walls that were falling off the outside of the White House. You would have seen beautiful ornamentation around the windows, where half of it was hanging off the window and the other half was up. Half of it, much of it, was actually gone. It was—it fell to the ground. It was removed. Fell to the ground, exploded, and it was removed. The place was in terrible shape. I made it beautiful.
You've seen the white marble floor, right? You've seen it, yeah. Nobody can do that. Very few people can do that. Well, I know how to do it. I made my money with luxury, and the White House, the White House, is a symbol of this country. Why should we have a White House—you know, when I came here, I was here maybe 20 years ago. I'll never forget. I came in. They had a meeting at the White House, and I came in and I looked at the walls as I got out of the car, and they were all broken, dented, the plaster was falling off them. That was 20 years ago. Now it's flawless.
[An aide comes in to say he has people waiting]
One thing, I just want to say this. I read a lot about, oh he's saying the White House was in very poor condition. It's now in better condition than when it was built. Could you give me those pictures, please? It's now in better condition than when it was built. Better, and it's not finished yet, but it's getting very close. And the White House is a symbol of America. When you look at a window and you see the ornamentation has fallen off half the window, or it's hanging from the final remaining screw that hasn't been rusted out.
Wiles: Or the chipping of the walls.
Trump: Oh the chipping. The walls? So bad. You know, over the course of 100 years, they were hit. I'll give you an example. Look at that board. See that woodwork? It's what I do best, I guess. Yeah. I say to people, am I a better builder or politician? See the walls. That wood was put there in 1901. It was in terrible condition. It was beat to shit. And what I did is I had it very gently by top top people stripped, Not easy to strip it and not destroy it. And there's a way of doing it that I can't tell you because that would be a whole other story. And look at it; it looks like it's in perfect condition. And then ended—solid gold. Look up and see the [unintelligible]. This office was in very bad condition. Now everyone loves it.
I know we got to get rolling. I do want to ask you. You know, you'd mentioned—
Here, just take a look. This was a while ago. This was work. This was 1949. Now, when I went through the court, they all said, "Oh, he's touching the White House.” This is the White House in 1949, 1949 means modern times.
You were three years old.
The White House was built in 1792, and the White House—look, this is the stairway going upstairs. That was in 1950. That's the stairway. This whole place was a wreck, and it was worse today. It was worse a year ago than it was here. It's just real fast. Now they said, they said, look, look at this, 1950. This is the interior of the White House. So when I do a little touch of a little paint, they say, "Oh, he's ruining the White House."
And I'll tell you, the East Wing was ripped down and rebuilt five times. That place, look at this. Just before it had—they changed the floor. If you want to do the floor, so that's in 1926. But the floor is terrible in here. If you want to do the floor, it's like a big deal. You want to put like a beautiful statuary or marble, which is the highest level. They'll say, "Oh, he's ruining the White House. Look at the condition of this place. So this is the East Room. Look, 1950, falling down. You see, that's where they had the event the other day for far too few people. Now, President Xi gave me a list, a lot of people. I said, if I give you that, I won't have anybody. Here's the State Dining Room in 1950, and I had to go through a courthouse with a judge who said, "You're destroying the White House.” It's the shit I have to go through. I brought it back to us, and I think the White House. See, there's your press room right there.
You mentioned the Democrats will come after you if they win. Are you considering pardoning members of your administration prior to the end of your term?
Yeah, sure I’d do that.
Is that something you would consider doing?
Well, Sleepy Joe Biden, he gave pardons to everyone. [Holds up pictures of White House] They're actually—see, this is the way it looks now.
Have you seen the videos of Mitch McConnell back in the Senate? Do you think he should resign because of his health condition?
It was a disappointment to a lot of Republicans. So that's just—well, Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody. He gave them to Fauci. He gave them to this. But you mean I'm not allowed to give them, but Sleepy Joe's allowed to give them? This ain't gonna be much of a story. Here we are doing this. You haven't asked me one fucking positive question. All of this. What about this? What about that? What about that? What about this? All negative. Why are you devoting all this time to the White House? You know how I do, I do that out of my back pocket. I pay for a lot of it, but I fix it because the White House should look like that. It shouldn’t look like—if you would have stood in that balcony and looked at that wall, half the wall was falling. It's actually dangerous. People are walking under, crap was falling off it all the time. Every time it rained, it was leaking, horrible. Now it's perfect, and I would say that I should be given credit for fixing the White House because I'm also doing very well with the war. I'm doing very well with another war that we already won, Venezuela. Do you notice you haven't asked me a question about Venezuela?
We did earlier.
No, no, I brought it up, and then you said—
You beat us to it. But yeah.
No, but I'm just thinking to myself, fake news. But I have a lot of respect. I like the owner, good guy. But I don't understand. I'm sitting here. I've done all this stuff. Look, this is nothing compared to what I've done, but I took the White House and made it beautiful again. Okay, and people look at it. People came up. President Xi looked at it two days ago. He said, "This is beautiful. Much better than I…" He was here 25 years ago with Obama. Think Obama knows it? Obama would not. He doesn't know if something's dirty or clean.
How did Xi's health seem to you? There are reports that Xi's in bad health. How did he seem to you?
I think he's in great health. I hope you quote me on that too, because I was with him for two days, extremely intense, a lot of visits to different places all over the place. I don't know, and he was in perfect health. I know when somebody’s not—
What will you miss the most about the White House?
This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office. I've been asking Susie for six months to give me a statement. Will we save this room? Will we make it a federal landmark?
No one can change what you've done to it, you're saying
No.
No one can tear it down.
I see the Secret Service looking, and I say, "What are you guys looking at?” “Sir, we think the Oval Office should be taken down, and we'll build a new one, sir.” I said, "My ass, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place.” The cabinet room too, which I also think—show them the cabinet room when they go out, okay. The cabinet room’s gorgeous. That was a mess. It was a disgusting mess. This whole place was a disgusting mess, and now it's perfect. But Joe didn't do it. Well, I hope I get a decent story. I don't think—you know, it's hard to get a good story. Every question's a hit. I don't know what the hell's wrong.
We really appreciate your time. Thank you.

articles.title: Giá USD hôm nay 1.10.2026: Đô la trong ngân hàng giảm
articles.text:
Các ngân hàng thương mại công bố giá USD ở mức thấp, Vietcombank giảm giá đô la Mỹ 10 đồng, mua vào 25.740 - 25.770 đồng, bán ra 26.150 đồng; ACB mua vào 25.750 - 25.780 đồng, bán ra 26.140 đồng; Vietinbank mua vào 25.595 đồng, bán ra 26.135 đồng… Các ngoại tệ khác trong ngân hàng tăng giảm trái chiều. Tại Vietcombank, giá EUR giảm 20 đồng, mua vào 28.669 - 28.959 đồng, bán ra 30.181 đồng; bảng Anh tăng 100 đồng, mua vào 33.561 - 33.900 đồng, bán ra 34.987 đồng...
Giá USD trên thị trường thế giới tăng nhẹ, chỉ số USD-Index thêm 0,1 điểm, lên 101,46 điểm. Đồng USD đi ngang so với các đồng tiền khác sau khi số liệu cho thấy lạm phát của Mỹ tăng thấp hơn dự kiến, qua đó làm giảm khả năng Cục Dự trữ liên bang Mỹ (Fed) tăng lãi suất.
Số liệu của Bộ Thương mại Mỹ cho thấy, chỉ số giá chi tiêu tiêu dùng cá nhân (PCE), thước đo lạm phát được Fed ưu tiên sử dụng, đã tăng 0,3% trong tháng trước. Các nhà kinh tế được Reuters khảo sát trước đó dự báo mức tăng 0,4%. Theo công cụ FedWatch của CME, các nhà giao dịch hiện đặt cược 37% khả năng Fed tăng lãi suất trong tháng 10, giảm mạnh so với mức 70% một tuần trước.
Các chuyên gia phân tích cho rằng, báo cáo về số liệu PCE yếu hơn dự kiến được công bố sau khi Chủ tịch Ngân hàng Dự trữ liên bang New York John Williams phản đối quan điểm cho rằng cần khẩn cấp thực hiện một đợt tăng lãi suất khác, đã khiến kỳ vọng về các đợt tăng lãi suất liên tiếp giảm đáng kể. Việc điều chỉnh lại kỳ vọng đang kéo lợi suất trái phiếu Kho bạc Mỹ xuống thấp hơn và thu hẹp lợi thế của đồng USD, thúc đẩy làn sóng bán USD mới nhất.
Lợi suất trái phiếu Kho bạc Mỹ trong bối cảnh kỳ vọng Fed sẽ tiếp tục tăng lãi suất ngày càng lớn, do lạm phát được thúc đẩy bởi giá dầu cao hơn. Đồng bạc xanh vẫn hướng tới mức tăng theo tháng so với đồng EUR, franc Thụy Sĩ và bảng Anh. Tuy nhiên, đồng USD đã mất một phần đà tăng sau khi dữ liệu được công bố. Lợi suất trái phiếu kỳ hạn 2 năm (loại trái phiếu thường biến động cùng chiều với kỳ vọng về lãi suất của Fed) đã giảm 0,4 điểm cơ bản xuống mức 4,885%.
